summary: JSON is a lightweight, text-based, language-independent data interchange format derived from the ECMAScript standard. It defines a small set of formatting rules for the portable representation of structured data. This document was replaced by RFC 7159.

eli5.summary: JSON is a simple way to write lists and labeled values as plain text so different programs can swap them. This version was replaced by RFC 7159.

questions: how do you write a json object
what characters must be escaped in json strings
how should json be parsed safely
subtitle: A text format for portable data interchange between programs

tldr.problem: Programs in different languages and on different platforms need to exchange structured data in a way that is simple to generate, parse, and read by humans.
tldr.mechanism: JSON defines a lightweight grammar with just six structural characters and a few value types: strings, numbers, booleans, nulls, objects (key-value collections), and arrays (ordered sequences). It is derived from JavaScript object syntax but excludes executable code.
tldr.outcome: JSON became ubiquitous for web APIs, configuration files, and data interchange across languages. This version fixed interoperability issues found in the original RFC 4627. RFC 7159 superseded it later.

today: RFC 7158 is an Internet Standard that repairs specification errors and clarifies interoperability best practices from the original RFC 4627. It was later superseded by RFC 7159 with similar scope. JSON has become the de facto standard for web APIs and data interchange across all programming languages and platforms.

sections.title: What JSON Is
sections.content:
JSON is a text format for sending structured data between programs. It was inspired by the object literals of the JavaScript programming language. JSON is minimal, portable, textual, and a subset of JavaScript, meaning JavaScript engines can parse it directly (though that approach is dangerous for untrusted data).

JSON can represent six kinds of values: four primitive types (strings, numbers, booleans, and null) and two structured types (objects and arrays). An object is an unordered collection of zero or more key-value pairs, where each key is a string and each value is any JSON value. An array is an ordered sequence of zero or more values.
sections.eli5: JSON is like a filing cabinet. Objects are drawers labeled with names, and arrays are numbered shelves. You can put anything in them: words, numbers, true/false, empty slots, or other filing cabinets and shelves.

sections.title: Grammar and Syntax
sections.content:
A JSON text is a sequence of tokens built from six structural characters: [ and ] for arrays, { and } for objects, : to separate keys from values, and , to separate elements. Whitespace (spaces, tabs, newlines, carriage returns) can appear before or after any structural character.

The entire JSON text is a single serialized value. Older specifications required that a JSON text be an object or array, but RFC 7158 allows any value (even a bare string or number) to be valid JSON text, as long as the implementation correctly handles it.

The literal names true, false, and null must be lowercase. No other literal names are allowed.
sections.eli5: JSON follows simple rules: use squigglies for lists of names and values, use square brackets for numbered lists, and use colons and commas to separate things. That's almost all you need to know.

sections.title: Data Types and Representation
sections.content:
Objects are surrounded by curly braces and contain zero or more name-value pairs separated by commas. Each name must be unique within the object (though SHOULD is the recommendation); when names are not unique, different implementations behave unpredictably.

Arrays are surrounded by square brackets and contain zero or more values separated by commas. The values in an array do not need to be the same type.

Strings are enclosed in quotation marks. They are sequences of Unicode characters. Most characters can be written directly, but certain characters must be escaped: the quotation mark itself, the backslash, and control characters (Unicode U+0000 through U+001F). The backslash notation includes two-character escapes like \n (newline) and six-character escapes like \uXXXX for Unicode code points.

Numbers are represented in base 10 without leading zeros. A number can have an optional minus sign, a decimal fraction (decimal point followed by digits), and an exponent (E or e followed by an optional plus or minus, followed by digits). Values like Infinity and NaN are not permitted in JSON.

Booleans are the literals true and false. Null is the literal null, representing the absence of a value.
sections.eli5: Put curly braces around name-value pairs, square brackets around lists, use backslashes to escape special characters in text, and write numbers the normal way. Three magic words are true, false, and null.

sections.title: Text Encoding and Interoperability
sections.content:
JSON text MUST be encoded in UTF-8, UTF-16, or UTF-32. UTF-8 is the default and strongly recommended because it offers the best interoperability; many implementations cannot read other encodings. Implementations MUST NOT add a byte order mark (BOM) to the beginning of JSON text, though parsers MAY tolerate one if present for compatibility.

When strings are composed entirely of valid Unicode characters (properly escaped), all implementations will agree on the meaning. However, ABNF in the spec allows some bit sequences that are not valid Unicode, such as unpaired UTF-16 surrogates. Software that receives such malformed text may crash, return different string lengths, or behave unpredictably. Implementers should be careful with string truncation.

RFC 7158 also clarifies that good interoperability is achieved when implementations handle number precision no more than IEEE 754 double-precision floating-point format (which has a 53-bit integer range). Numbers larger than that range are legal JSON but may cause interoperability problems.
sections.eli5: Write JSON in UTF-8 text (the most common encoding for text files). Some unusual numbers or escaped characters might not work the same in every program, so stick to simple values if you can.

sections.title: Security Notes
sections.content:
JSON syntax is deliberately a subset of JavaScript to enable easy parsing, but that same property creates a danger: an untrusted JSON text could be executed by a JavaScript interpreter using an unsafe mechanism, allowing malicious code to run. The correct approach is to use a dedicated JSON parser, not a language interpreter. Most modern frameworks provide safe JSON parsing libraries that extract data without executing any code.

Another consideration: JSON is a data-only format with no executable content, so it is inherently safer than formats that include code. However, applications that process JSON should still validate that the data is well-formed and has the expected structure.
sections.eli5: Use a proper JSON parser to read JSON data, not a code interpreter. That way someone cannot hide code inside the data that could run on your computer.
